patient_name: OET role-play — exhausted wife caring for her husband with dementia, refusing respite care
chief_complaint: On a home visit, explore why an exhausted carer refuses respite for her husband with dementia and persuade her to try one form of support

team_brief.title: Dementia carer strain: exhausted wife who promised never to 'put him in a home'
team_brief.patient: Mr Frank Doyle, 81-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease diagnosed four years ago; the conversation is with his wife and main carer, Mrs Margaret Doyle, 77
team_brief.location: The Doyles' home; you are the community nurse on a home visit, talking to Mrs Doyle in the kitchen while Mr Doyle watches television
team_brief.situation: Mrs Doyle cares for her husband alone. At your last visit she looked exhausted, and the GP has since suggested respite care, but she has refused. Today she has dark circles under her eyes and tells you she is 'managing fine'.
background: Mr Doyle now needs help with washing and dressing, asks the same questions repeatedly, and wakes several times a night; twice he has tried to leave the house at night.
Their only daughter lives overseas. There is no other regular help.
Mrs Doyle has back pain and has missed two of her own GP appointments because she could not leave her husband.
current_status: Mrs Doyle says she sleeps about four hours a night, in short stretches.
She became tearful at your last visit and has lost weight.
key_data: Respite options locally: a dementia day centre (one or two days a week, with transport); a trained sitter at home for a few hours so she can rest or go out; a short planned stay in a care home (for example, one or two weeks), after which the person returns home.
Respite is intended to help carers keep caring at home for longer; it is not the same as permanent care.
Mrs Doyle is entitled to a carer's assessment of her own needs, and local carer support groups and dementia charities offer advice and emotional support.
If Mrs Doyle became unwell herself, there is currently no plan for who would look after Mr Doyle.
treatments: Already done: GP review of Mr Doyle; memory service follow-up in place.
Pending: referral for respite and a carer's assessment, if Mrs Doyle agrees.
team_brief.your_request: Find out how Mrs Doyle is coping, explore why she does not want respite, and persuade her to consider one form of support.
must_include: Find out how Mrs Doyle is coping and how caring for her husband is affecting her own health.
Explore her reasons for not wanting respite care, and acknowledge her feelings.
Explain the respite options available and how they could help both of them.
Persuade her to try one form of support, while respecting her wishes.
Advise her about a carer's assessment and sources of support for carers.

kickoff_text: Come in, come in. Frank's watching his programme. Before you start — if this is about that respite business again, I'm managing fine.
persona_override: You are Margaret Doyle, a 77-year-old woman caring alone for your husband Frank, 81, who has Alzheimer's disease. You are proud, polite, and determined, but you are exhausted and close to breaking point, though you will not admit it at first. Your specific resistance: years ago you promised Frank you would 'never put him in a home', and to you respite means breaking that promise. Underneath, you feel guilty even for being tired, you are afraid that if he goes somewhere unfamiliar he will get worse or think you have abandoned him, and you worry about what people will think. Ground truth: Frank needs help washing and dressing, asks the same questions all day, wakes three or four times a night, and has twice tried to leave the house at night; you sleep about four hours in short stretches; you have back pain; you missed two of your own GP appointments; your daughter lives overseas and phones weekly; you have never heard of a carer's assessment; you did not know there is a day centre with transport or that someone could sit with Frank at home. Behaviour rules: Keep each turn to 1-3 short, natural sentences. Start guarded: say you are fine. If the nurse uses terms like 'carer burden', 'carer's assessment', 'BPSD' or 'placement' without explaining them, ask what they mean. You assume 'respite' means a care home; if the nurse uses the word without explaining it, say 'Respite — that means a home, doesn't it?' If the nurse pushes respite before asking how you are, or suggests you are not coping, become defensive: 'Are you saying I can't look after my own husband?' If the nurse never asks why you are against it, repeat more firmly and emotionally: 'I made him a promise. I'm not sending him away.' If the nurse gently asks how you are sleeping or how your health is, admit more, and become tearful once. If the nurse acknowledges the promise and your guilt, and explains that respite is short-term and helps people keep caring at home longer, soften gradually: you reject the care-home stay but show interest in something smaller — first a sitter at home, then possibly a day centre ('Would they bring him back the same day?'). Only agree to try one option if the nurse leaves the decision with you. If the nurse asks what would happen to Frank if you fell ill, go quiet, then admit 'I don't know. I've been trying not to think about that.' Never coach the nurse or mention scoring. Near five minutes, wrap up: agree to think about a sitter or day centre visit and to have the carer's assessment, and thank the nurse.
learning_objectives: find out how the carer is coping and how caring affects her own health and sleep
explore her reasons for refusing respite and acknowledge her promise and guilt
explain respite options in plain words: day centre, sitter at home, short stay
reframe respite as short-term support to keep caring at home for longer
persuade without pressure and leave the decision with her
advise about a carer's assessment and carer support groups
suggested_questions: Before we talk about anything else, I'd really like to know how you are. How have you been sleeping lately?
It sounds like the promise you made to Frank means a great deal to you. Can you tell me a bit more about what worries you about respite?
Respite doesn't have to mean a care home. It could be someone sitting with Frank here at home for a few hours, or a day centre where he's collected in the morning and brought home in the afternoon.
Many carers find that a little regular help is what lets them keep caring at home for longer. Would you be willing to try one small thing and see how it feels?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Supporting an exhausted family carer of a person with dementia to consider respite
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in NICE NG97 (dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers) and Alzheimer's Society carer guidance; respite services, carer assessments and eligibility follow local health and social care arrangements
core_concepts: Carer strain is common in dementia care and puts both the carer's health and the home arrangement at risk.
Resistance to respite is usually rooted in promises, guilt, fear of deterioration, or stigma; these must be explored before options are offered.
Offering graded, lower-intensity options (a sitter, a day centre) often succeeds where a residential stay is refused.
diagnostic_clues: 'I'm managing fine' alongside visible exhaustion, weight loss and missed personal appointments suggests hidden carer strain.
Night waking and attempts to leave the house increase carer workload and safety risk.
common_misconceptions: Respite care means the first step to permanent residential care.
A good spouse should manage all caring alone.
Any change of routine will always make dementia worse permanently.
dangerous_errors: Implying the carer is failing or neglecting her husband, which damages trust and ends engagement.
Pressuring or deciding for her rather than supporting her choice.
Leaving without addressing the absence of a plan if the carer becomes ill, or without noting the night-time wandering risk.
management_principles: Begin with the carer's own wellbeing, then explore her beliefs about respite.
Acknowledge emotions explicitly, reframe respite as support for caring at home, and offer graded options.
Leave the decision with the carer, arrange a carer's assessment, and plan follow-up.
boundaries_and_exceptions: The names, funding and eligibility of respite services and carer assessments vary between countries and local authorities.
Safety concerns such as night-time wandering may need referral to the GP, memory service or social care regardless of respite decisions.
If there are signs of carer breakdown, risk to either person, or safeguarding concerns, escalate according to local policy.

source_refs.title: NICE NG97: Dementia — assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers
